name: Forum of Trajan
summary: The last and biggest of Rome’s imperial forums, a huge square lined with columns and paid for with the loot from the Dacian Wars. It was dedicated in AD 112, and a gilded bronze statue of Trajan on horseback stood in the middle.

name: Basilica Ulpia
summary: A giant hall full of columns along the north-west side of the forum, used for law courts and public business. It was named after Trajan’s family, the Ulpii, and was one of the biggest basilicas Rome ever had.

name: Trajan's Column
summary: A marble column 100 Roman feet (about 30 m) tall, wrapped in a spiral of about 155 scenes from the two Dacian Wars. It was dedicated in May 113, and after Trajan died his ashes were put in a golden urn inside its base.

name: Markets of Trajan
summary: A brick building of several floors full of shops, halls and offices, built into the side of the Quirinal Hill next to the forum. The name is modern. Besides shops, it probably held offices for running the city.

name: Baths of Trajan
summary: Enormous public baths on the Oppian Hill, built on top of part of Nero’s Golden House and opened in June 109. The layout, with the bathing halls in the middle of a big walled park, was copied by later emperors like Caracalla and Diocletian.

name: Aqua Traiana
place: From springs near Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum, Rome (pin at the Janiculum)
summary: An aqueduct that carried spring water almost 60 km from the hills around Lake Bracciano to the Janiculum Hill. It supplied the neighbourhood across the Tiber and turned water mills, and it opened on 24 June 109, two days after the Baths of Trajan.

name: Portus, Trajan’s six-sided harbour
summary: Trajan dug a six-sided harbour behind the older harbour of Claudius near the mouth of the Tiber. Each side is about 358 m long, and a canal joined it to the river. It made Portus the main port for the grain ships that fed Rome.

name: Via Traiana
place: Beneventum to Brundisium, southern Italy (pin at Canusium, about halfway)
summary: A new road from Beneventum to Brundisium that Trajan paid for himself. It was shorter and easier than the old Via Appia, running through towns like Aecae, Canusium, Barium and Egnatia.

name: Arch of Trajan, Benevento
summary: A triumphal arch voted by the Senate in 114, standing where the Via Traiana left Beneventum. Its carved panels are some of the best preserved on any Roman arch, and they celebrate what Trajan did for Rome, Italy and the provinces.

name: Arch of Trajan, Ancona
summary: A tall, thin marble arch on the harbour wall at Ancona, put up by the Senate and people around 115. The inscription thanks Trajan for making the harbour safer for sailors and paying for it himself.

name: Harbour of Ancona
summary: Trajan enlarged Ancona’s harbour on the Adriatic with a new breakwater, which improved Italy’s main crossing to Dalmatia and the Danube provinces. A harbour scene on the column is often said to be Ancona.

name: Trajan's Bridge over the Danube
summary: A bridge over 1,100 m long, with 20 stone piers holding up a wooden roadway, built so the army could cross into Dacia for the second war. For over a thousand years it was probably the longest arch bridge in the world, and stumps of its piers still stand on both banks.

name: Tabula Traiana and the Iron Gates road
place: Iron Gates gorge of the Danube, Serbia
summary: A plaque carved into the cliffs of the Danube gorge says Trajan’s engineers finished a road here in AD 100, cut into the rock and partly carried on a wooden walkway over the water. When the Iron Gates dam raised the river in the 1960s and 70s, the plaque was moved higher up the cliff.

name: Alcántara Bridge
summary: A granite bridge of six arches over the river Tagus, about 45 m high. Local towns paid for it and dedicated it to Trajan. An inscription names its builder, Gaius Julius Lacer, and cars still drive over it today.
latinNote: Its Latin name is not known; Alcántara comes from the Arabic for "the bridge".

name: Tropaeum Traiani
summary: A huge round victory monument, about 40 m across, dedicated to Mars the Avenger in 109 after the Dacian Wars. Its 54 carved panels show Roman soldiers fighting Dacians and their allies, and a Roman town with the same name grew up next to it.

name: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa
latin: Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa
summary: The first Roman colony in Dacia and the capital of the new province, founded for retired soldiers by the governor Decimus Terentius Scaurianus. It sat about 40 km west of the ruined Dacian royal city, Sarmizegetusa Regia, and borrowed its name.

name: Thamugadi (Timgad)
summary: A town for retired soldiers founded in AD 100 by the Third Augustan Legion, laid out on a perfect grid near the Aurès mountains. Its streets, forum and theatre survive so well that it’s the textbook example of a Roman town. The so-called Arch of Trajan there was built later.

name: Via Nova Traiana
place: Province of Arabia: Bostra to Aila (pin at Petra)
summary: A paved road through the new province of Arabia, built under the governor Gaius Claudius Severus. It ran more than 400 km from Bostra down to Aila (Aqaba) on the Red Sea, and its milestones say it went “from the borders of Syria to the Red Sea”.

name: Harbour of Centumcellae
summary: A new harbour on the coast north-west of Rome, sheltered by two curved breakwaters and a man-made island at its mouth. Pliny the Younger watched it being built while he stayed at Trajan’s villa there, and he wrote about it in a letter.

name: Trajan's Kiosk, Philae
summary: An open pavilion of 14 columns next to the Temple of Isis. It’s called Trajan’s Kiosk because carvings inside show Trajan making offerings to Egyptian gods, though the building may have been started earlier, maybe under Augustus. In the 1970s it was moved, with the rest of Philae’s temples, to save it from the rising water behind the Aswan dams.

name: Italica (Trajan's birthplace)
summary: The Roman town in southern Spain where, according to most ancient writers, Trajan was born in AD 53 to a family of settlers from Italy. Founded in 206 BC, it was the first Roman town in Spain. Hadrian, whose family also came from here, later rebuilt much of it and added a temple to Trajan.
note: Birthplace, not a Trajanic building project.
